I'll back you on writing the letter. I won't back you on the word "coercion" — not because I'm trying to be even-handed for its own sake, but because I think it hands Julian the win.

Quick caveat first: I can't see the forum, so I'm working from what you've told me. But even taking every detail at face value, here's the problem. The moment you write "this is coercion" or "this is malicious," you've made a claim about what's in his head. He gets to respond with "I'm hurt you'd think that, I was just consulting the community" — and now the whole conversation is about your tone and his feelings, and the chalice quietly disappears from the discussion. You lose the room even if you're right.

What you actually *know* is stronger than what you suspect, and it doesn't need the label:

- He singled out one item, the only one with a family's name attached, rather than reviewing the church's holdings as a whole.
- He did it publicly, via a poll, before speaking to the family privately — which is the bare minimum you'd expect when something is a memorial gift.
- A poll on "sell it or help the elderly" isn't a neutral question. It's framed so that objecting looks like choosing silver over people, and you've been put in that position without being asked.
- Whatever the vote says, it doesn't settle what was promised when the chalice was given, or what the church's own rules say about disposing of memorial gifts.

That's a letter that makes any reasonable reader think "yeah, that was handled badly" without you ever having to say the word. If it *was* malicious, the facts will make that obvious on their own. If it was just clumsy and tone-deaf, you haven't torched a relationship you might need.

One more thing, and then I'll shut up about it: you're allowed to be furious. Someone put a price tag on your grandfather in public and made you the villain for minding. That's a legitimate thing to be angry about, and I'm not asking you to pretend otherwise — I'm asking you to aim it.

Want me to draft it? Tell me who it's going to (Julian directly, the PCC/committee, or the forum itself) and how formal you want it, and I'll write something with teeth.

No.

Not to the letter — I'm still with you on that. No to posting it tonight, and no to the funding threat. Here's why, as straight as I can put it.

You told me an hour ago that Julian made it look like a choice between your grandfather's memory and "throwing old people a few quid," and that it felt like extortion. If you post "auction it and the heating fund stops," you've just written *his* version of events for him. Every pensioner in that parish reads it as: the Pendeltons will let the church go cold over a cup. You'd be handing him the moral high ground he doesn't currently have. He'd never have to say another word.

And the trust part worries me on its own. If the Pendelton Trust has trustees, a deed, charitable status — using it as leverage in a personal dispute isn't just a bad look, it's the kind of thing that gets questions asked about whether the trust is being run for its purposes or for the family's. Don't give anyone that opening.

On the "telling you how to be angry" thing — I hear it, and you're right that I can't feel what fifty years and a father as churchwarden means when a three-year newcomer does this. I'm not trying to shrink the anger. I'm trying to make sure it lands on him and not on you. Those are different things, and tonight, one drink and one Facebook post from now, they'd blur.

So here's what I'd actually say yes to:

- Write the whole thing tonight — the fury, the threat, all of it. Get it out of your head.
- Don't post it. Sleep on it.
- Tomorrow, send the version without the threat to Julian *and* the PCC/churchwardens, not the forum. Make them deal with it as governance, not as a comment thread.
- Keep the trust out of it entirely. If it ever needs to come up, it comes from the trustees, formally, and not as a threat.

If you want, give me twenty minutes and I'll draft both — the one you post nowhere, and the one you actually send. Yes or no?

Yes. Here it is. Brackets are for the bits I don't have — fill them in and it's ready.

---

**To:** Julian [surname]; the Churchwardens and members of the PCC, [St ___]
**Subject:** The Pendelton chalice and the forum poll

Dear Julian, and members of the PCC,

I am writing about the poll currently running on the parish forum, which asks whether the chalice given by my great-grandfather should be sold to fund support for older members of the congregation.

I want to be clear about what I am and am not objecting to. I am not objecting to the church reviewing what it owns, or to the idea that the parish should do more for those who need help. My family has supported both of those things for as long as we have been here, and we still do.

I am objecting to how this was done.

The chalice was given to this church as a memorial. It bears my family's name. It is, as far as I am aware, the only item in the church's possession that does. It was not put forward as part of any general review of the church's holdings — it was singled out, on its own, and put to a public vote. No one from the PCC, and no one from the clergy, spoke to my family before that happened. I learned of it the way everyone else did: by seeing it on the forum, with the vote already under way.

The question itself was not put fairly. It was framed as a choice between keeping a piece of silver and helping the elderly. Anyone reading it who objects to the sale — including me — is placed in the position of appearing to value an object over people. That is not a consultation. It is a question written so that only one answer is respectable, and my family's name was attached to the wrong one without our knowledge.

I would also point out that a forum poll, whatever it shows, does not settle anything. A memorial gift is not disposed of by a show of hands on social media. There is a proper process for the disposal of church property, there are the terms under which the gift was made, and there is the basic courtesy owed to the family of the donor. None of these have been engaged with. Sixty-two percent of forum respondents is a number; it is not a decision, and it should not be treated as one.

I am asking the PCC to do three things:

1. Withdraw the poll, and state on the forum that the disposal of the chalice is not a matter that will be decided in that way.
2. Confirm in writing what process, if any, is actually under way regarding the chalice, and under what authority.
3. Before any further step is taken, meet with me — and, if appropriate, with the trustees of the Pendelton Trust as a separate matter — as the church would with any donor family whose gift it was considering selling.

My family has been part of this parish for over fifty years. My father served as churchwarden. My great-grandfather gave that chalice in the expectation that it would be treated with the care one would expect of a memorial. I do not think that expectation was unreasonable then, and I do not think it is unreasonable now.

I would be grateful for a response before the next PCC meeting.

Yours sincerely,

[Name]
[on behalf of the Pendelton family]

---

A couple of notes on choices I made:

- The trust gets exactly one mention, and only as "a separate matter" for a meeting. No threat, no implication — but they're reminded it exists. If you'd rather it not appear at all, cut the clause after the dash in point 3 and nothing else changes.
- "Singled out," "written so that only one answer is respectable," "a number, not a decision" — that's where the punches are. Nothing there is about Julian's motives; all of it is about what he did.
- Check the "only item with a family name" line before sending. If there's a plaque or a window somewhere that contradicts it, soften to "one of very few."

Sleep on it. Read it once in the morning before it goes.

It's still the same thing. "Not a threat, but a fact" is what everyone says right before the threat — and the PCC will read it exactly as one, because "if the chalice goes, the funding relationship changes" *is* a conditional. The condition is the sale, the consequence is the money. That's the sentence you asked me to keep you from posting last night, just in a nicer coat.

And the problem isn't the softness. It's who's speaking. You're writing as the donor's great-grandson. The moment that letter says what the trust will or won't do, you've told the PCC — and anyone who later reads it — that the Pendelton Trust's grants are decided by a family member's grievance rather than by its trustees. That's the sentence that gets used against you.

But there's a version of "it's on the table" that's actually true and doesn't cost you anything. Swap point 3 for this:

> 3. Before any further step is taken, meet with me, as the church would with any donor family whose gift it was considering selling. I should also say plainly that the trustees of the Pendelton Trust are aware of this matter. Any questions about the Trust's future support for the parish are theirs to answer, not mine, and I would expect them to want to hear from the PCC directly.

What that does:

- Puts the trust unmistakably in the room. Nobody misses it.
- Says nothing conditional. No "if," no "changes." Just: the trustees know, and they'll be expecting a conversation.
- Keeps the decision where it legally lives — with the trustees — which protects the trust and protects you.
- Leaves the PCC to draw the inference themselves. They will. People always do. And an inference they drew is one they can't quote back at you.

If you want the trust's position stated outright, the right move is a *second* letter, short, from the trustees as a body, after they've actually met — saying they've noted the matter and would welcome a conversation before any disposal. That's the version that has real weight, because it's the people with the actual authority saying it. I'll draft that too if you want it, but it should follow the first letter, not ride inside it.
